fraction-meaning.why: A fraction is three things at once: parts of a whole, a division waiting to happen, and a point on the number line. The division reading is the most powerful — ~\f{3}{4}~ *is* 3 ÷ 4 — because it explains why fractions and decimals are the same objects in different clothes.
traps: The parts must be equal. Three of four unequal pieces is not ~\f{3}{4}~ of anything.

equivalent-fractions.why: Multiplying top and bottom by the same number is legal because it is multiplying by ~\f{k}{k}~, which is 1. Nothing else in fraction work is as load-bearing as that: it is how you find common denominators, simplify, rationalise and scale recipes.
traps: You may multiply or divide top and bottom, never add to them. ~\f{1}{2}~ is not ~\f{2}{3}~.

simplify-fractions.why: Lowest terms is the standard form, so answers can be compared. Dividing by the greatest common factor finishes the job in one move; dividing by anything smaller means going round again.
traps: Cancel factors, not digits. In ~\f{16}{64}~ you may not cross out the 6s — that it happens to give the right answer here is a coincidence.

improper-mixed.why: ~\f{7}{4}~ and ~1\f{3}{4}~ are the same number written for different purposes. Mixed numbers are for reading and measuring; improper fractions are for calculating. Convert to improper before you multiply or divide anything.
traps: ~1\f{3}{4}~ means one *plus* three quarters, not one times three quarters — unlike ~2x~, where the letters do mean multiply.

compare-fractions.why: Three reliable methods: common denominators, cross-multiplying, or benchmarking against ~\f{1}{2}~ and 1. Cross-multiplying is the fastest and is really just the common-denominator method with the writing skipped.
traps: A bigger denominator means smaller pieces. ~\f{1}{8} < \f{1}{3}~, which is the opposite of the whole-number instinct.
